extracted.intended_audience: early-career academic mathematicians / new university faculty
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative standards for university-level mathematics teaching (preparation, delivery, evaluation, course management, textbook selection, and reputation-building) aimed at early-career faculty and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of professional duties
rubrics_metrics.description: An academic mathematician's work includes (i) research, (ii) exposition, (iii) Departmental administrative activities, (iv) University administrative activities, (v) service to the profession; teaching is important but is by no means the only thing and is well less than half of what you do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep all components in perspective and apportion time appropriately: do not give all your time to teaching (which will harm research) or to research (which will harm other duties). Tenure and advancement evaluate multiple characteristics, so maintain a balanced portfolio of activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take teaching seriously / treat teaching as primary visible work
rubrics_metrics.description: Take your teaching seriously—it's the most visible thing you do, affects departmental reputation, credibility with administration, and 'pays the bills.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for more than an average teaching record: preparation and pedagogy matter for promotion and institutional standing. Being a creditable and visible teacher is professionally valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a personal, evolving teaching style
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching is a personal activity; you will need to develop your own values, goals, and methods and hone them over your professional life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with different didactic methods (jocular vs serious, guide-on-the-side vs sage-on-the-stage) and adopt what works for you; expect continual refinement across your career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek mentors and peer feedback for teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: It is worthwhile to have a teaching mentor chosen from among the senior faculty and to brainstorm with peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult experienced colleagues about class management, exams, lectures on tricky topics, graphics, technology, and department-specific expectations. Peer mentoring and discussing issues with other junior faculty helps resolve common problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-investing in teaching to the exclusion of other duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not develop the reputation of someone who does teaching to the exclusion of all else (e.g., hanging out with students night and day, spending untold hours preparing extra lessons and handouts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive time on teaching can signal lack of perspective or immaturity to colleagues and may harm your broader career prospects; carry your weight without becoming the caricature 'teaching type' unless that is a conscious, accepted career choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare lectures, syllabus, assignments, and exams carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a good syllabus; prepare each lecture or classroom lesson carefully and in detail; write neat, clear, coherent assignments and exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice delivery, make lectures shine, and arrange for colleagues or friends to observe and give constructive remarks. Videotaping via a Teaching Center can be revealing and useful for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be fair, reliable, punctual, and available to students
rubrics_metrics.description: Make yourself available to students; be fair, reliable, and punctual so students can depend on you and not be 'surprised in nasty ways.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat students the way you'd like to be treated: prepare lessons, show good attitude, treat everyone with dignity and respect, be helpful, and exert effort to be evenhanded—these practices foster student respect and forgiveness for other shortcomings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage classroom disruptions with composure and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: When disruptions occur (stupid questions, books dropped, pizza deliveries, cell phones), turn the situation into a plus rather than moralizing or harsh punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wit or light responses to keep atmosphere positive and avoid alienating the class; emulate hosts who 'roll with the punches' to maintain morale and contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt teaching to students' preparation and local curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust presentation and level to the students and the way the curriculum is structured; instructors from other systems may need special pains to acquaint themselves with local expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to students' backgrounds and goals; failing to adapt (e.g., teaching as if to advanced juniors in introductory classes) will not work—learn department and institutional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third-party input for teaching evaluation (student & peer evaluations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching is commonly evaluated via student teaching evaluation questionnaires; chairs often send faculty to observe teaching; mid-term evaluations and peer observations are common; self-evaluation is the least reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect objective third-party assessments: student evaluations (now often online), mid-term confidential feedback, and peer classroom observations provide actionable data. Do not rely on self-assessment; use external input to improve and document teaching effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mid-term evaluations and confidential feedback to improve courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many schools have mid-term teaching evaluations (between students and instructor, often with no records kept) which are useful for finding out how the course is going and what can be improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mid-term checks are valuable as they allow instructors to adjust pacing, clarity, and methods before it is too late; implement them where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a teaching reputation through student praise, seminars, and service
rubrics_metrics.description: Outstanding teaching reputation spreads by word-of-mouth; unsolicited student letters, active seminar participation, starting a teaching seminar, and serving on undergraduate or curriculum committees build reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in departmental teaching initiatives carefully (run seminars as intelligent exchanges, volunteer for committees) and be mindful that a strong teaching reputation changes how colleagues view your role in research/hiring contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of career trade-offs and evolving roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Spending most of your time on teaching is valid but will 'peg' you as a teaching-type; as careers progress, focus may shift from research to service and teaching roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make conscious choices about career direction; institutions expect research focus early and more service later—balance accordingly and recognize institutional expectations for promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage large lectures with specific strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-lecture teaching (e.g., 300 students) is difficult; instructors should use techniques to bring life into large classes and mitigate problems with recitation sections taught by TAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appoint ombudsmen to open communication, hold extra office hours and review sessions, coordinate with recitation TAs, and take steps to maintain order and student engagement; expect grading and homework collection challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate multi-lecturer/large-course logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: In cooperative large-course scenarios (multiple lectures + many recitations), faculty should meet regularly to discuss management of TAs, exam construction/scheduling/proctoring, grading, pacing, overall grading policies, office hours, and math lab coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a common syllabus, give common exams, coordinate grading and office hours, and stick to a disciplined lesson plan so students can attend alternate lectures without falling behind—cooperation saves labor and improves consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose textbooks meticulously and be mindful of departmental/publisher dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook choice strongly affects course quality: consider style (reform vs traditional), emphasis (computational vs applications), clarity, exercise design, error rates, and availability; be aware of department textbook selection policies and publisher influence (sales reps, inducements, and potential bribes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to vet texts via colleagues, reviews (AMS Monthly, Mathematical Gazette), and online feedback before adoption; avoid illegal photocopying/compilation of multiple texts into a sold reader; be careful with publisher inducements and respect departmental adoption procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when cobbling or replacing texts mid-semester
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandoning a text mid-semester or compiling disparate materials can create problems for students (cost, continuity) and legal/copyright issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not change core texts mid-term unless necessary; avoid creating bound readers from photocopied material that violate copyright—consult university policies and the department before adopting unconventional solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use media thoughtfully and weigh pros/cons
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation media have evolved (chalk, overheads, PowerPoint, electronic methods) and affect visibility, polish, preparation time, archival reuse, and graphics presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose media appropriate to the audience and content: slides/overheads make materials visible and polished and can be archived, but require extra prep time; be mindful of trade-offs in preparation time versus pedagogical benefits.
